text: Lipschitz stability for identification of piecewise constant conductivity coefficient in parabolic equation from finitely many interior point measurements The fundamental solution of a divergence-form parabolic equation with a measurable, uniformly elliptic coefficient matrix satisfies a specific derivative estimate. The coefficient matrix is assumed to be Lipschitz continuous in the spatial variable. The constants in the estimate depend only on the ellipticity constant, the dimension, and the Lipschitz constant. Under given conditions, the unique solution to the parabolic equation with initial condition linear in x is Lipschitz continuous in both time and space. The Lipschitz constant depends on the slope parameter theta. This constant is given by a function kappa of theta, which is locally bounded. The result holds for all real values of theta. For a constant p between 1 and infinity, assume the coefficients a are continuous with specified moduli of continuity on different parts of the domain. For any f in L_p, there exists a unique strong solution u in the Sobolev space W^{1,2}_p to the given parabolic equation with zero Dirichlet boundary condition. The solution satisfies an estimate where its norm is bounded by a constant times the norm of f. The constant depends only on the dimension, p, the ellipticity constant, and the moduli of continuity. Under certain conditions on the functions A and H, a solution u to a parabolic equation with bounded initial data and a time derivative bounded below remains Lipschitz continuous in space. The Lipschitz constant depends on the spatial domain and parameters from the problem. It is expressed in terms of given constants and the bounds on the solution and its derivatives. The constant K_r is explicitly given and depends only on the dimension and a parameter m.

title: Learned initializer + log-space Gauss-Newton/LM refinement reaches near the Cramér–Rao floor
text: The map theta -> F(theta) is smooth and locally well-conditioned (median Fisher condition 48), with noise sigma=1e-3. So a few LM steps started from a cheap data-driven estimate converge to the per-sample MLE. The MLE's error should approach the CRB rel_l2 floor of about 0.019. Hybrid kernel_ridge init with 10 LM iterations in log(k) will give val rel_l2 < 0.035, at least 5x better than any pure library regressor of similar cost. The forward operator is a 4-parameter, cheap, fully known explicit FD solver. The diagnostics show every parameter is locally identifiable, with CRB relative std between 0.005 and 0.022. A purely learned regressor trained on 3000 samples in a 4-D box has approximation error that likely sits well above the CRB. Local Gauss-Newton removes that approximation error, provided it starts inside the basin of attraction. A learned initializer supplies that start and avoids the cost of multistart. A log transform matches the multiplicative scale of conductivity, enforces positivity, and makes the Jacobian columns more uniform across [0.5, 2]. k1 and k4 are the least determined because their segments are far from the Gaussian pulse at x=0.5, so heat reaches them late and weakly. The harness forward model is the same simulator that generated the data: same grid, dt, initial condition and sensor indices. The explicit scheme is stable for k up to 2: dt*k_max/dx^2 <= 1/2. Misfit has a single dominant basin around the truth over most of the box; kernel ridge init lands inside it. Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian, so unweighted least squares is the MLE.

The hypothesis is refuted if val rel_l2 >= 0.035, or if refinement improves on the init by less than 2x. Either outcome would indicate bad basins, inconsistency between the forward model and the data, or failure of LM convergence.

title: Bayesian MMSE (posterior mean under the box prior) beats the MLE on rel_l2 because CRB-limited segments k1 and k4 benefit from prior shrinkage
text: rel_l2 is a squared-error-type loss. The prior is known exactly (i.i.d. uniform on [0.5, 2]). So the posterior mean is the Bayes-optimal estimator and is not bound by the unbiased CRB. Pure physics LM in log space with multistart 3, followed by importance-sampled posterior mean on the Laplace approximation, will reach val rel_l2 < 0.03. It will also be at least 5% better than the same pipeline with estimator=mode, with the gain concentrated in k1 and k4 and in samples near the box bounds. The CRB applies only to unbiased estimators. With a bounded uniform prior, the MLE projected onto the box is biased near the bounds and has high variance in the weakly observed edge segments. The MMSE estimator under the true prior minimizes expected squared error, so in expectation it cannot be worse than the MLE. The Laplace approximation is accurate because the posterior is nearly Gaussian at sigma=1e-3 and cond about 48, and importance sampling corrects for box truncation. Multistart replaces the learned init and tests whether the misfit landscape is unimodal enough for physics alone. This proposal needs no training data at all, which also separates physics error from learning error. The prior stated in the problem is the true data-generating prior for val and test. The posterior is close to Gaussian in log(k) near the mode, so a Laplace proposal gives low-variance importance weights. Multistart with 3 starts finds the global mode for most samples. The forward model matches the data generator.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Amortised-then-exact: an MLP on log features as a global initialiser, LM posterior-mean refinement as the corrector
text: A purely data-driven regressor (torch MLP on log-temperature features, with log targets) will stall well above the CRB floor, at val rel_l2 around 0.04-0.08, because 3000 samples are too few to learn the inverse map to noise-limited precision in 4D. Using that same network only as an initialiser for 10 LM iterations with the posterior-mean correction will cut its val rel_l2 by at least 40%, landing below 0.03. It will do this with fewer forward evaluations than cold-start physics, because the learned initialiser removes the need for multistarts. This combines two traditions: amortised simulation-based inference and classical variational data assimilation. Each has a characteristic failure. The network is robust globally, but its precision is limited by approximation and estimation error. LM is precise locally, but it can be trapped in a poor basin when started far away. The proposal tests whether these failures are complementary. Log features make sense physically: the solution decays roughly exponentially in time at rates that scale with k, so log u is closer to linear in log k. The task could be framed as 'choose the best regressor', but the network actually only needs to land within the LM basin of attraction. If that is true, a cheap network is enough and the remaining error is set by the likelihood rather than the learner. The MLP's errors are small enough (relative error up to about 10%) that LM converges to the global basin from the MLP's estimate. The log feature transform is defined: sensor readings stay positive or are shifted/clipped by the harness. Near-zero late-time readings with noise of 1e-3 could make log features noisy or undefined. If the harness clips them, information may be distorted. Training data come from the same simulator as the val data and from the same prior, so the amortised initialiser has no distribution shift. LM refinement cost with 10 iterations and no extra starts fits within the 120 s per-experiment limit alongside MLP training.
